# Atomization brief (shared by every Flint ingest agent)

Read this whole file before writing anything. It holds the rules the Harries review taught (2026-09-26: 25 of 35 files needed fixes). The review gate will check every rule here.

## Schema

Follow `C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\ingest-book\SKILL.md` exactly: `_domain.md`, `_book.md` (map and resume checkpoint, updated after EACH chapter or unit), and entries named `<kind>--<kebab-slug>.md` with kind one of principle, framework, case-study, heuristic, claim. Use the frontmatter keys exactly as the skill gives them. The body has **What it is** / **Why it works** / **When to apply** / **When NOT to apply** (mandatory, non-trivial) / **Example** / **Related**.

Style reference, read before writing: `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library\strength-and-conditioning\fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer\case-study--isometric-sprinter-and-hurdler.md`, plus one principle file in the same folder.

## Voices: label every one

- **The source author's statements are plain text.**
- **Eric's views** (from `docs/method-baseline.md` or his reviews) are prefixed "Eric's baseline:" or "Eric's review:".
- **Your own reasoning, application or synthesis** is prefixed "Inference:".
- **Nothing unlabeled that the author did not say.** The most common failures: a judgment from Eric's review written as if the author said it; a mechanism the author never gave presented as "why it works" (write "The author gives no mechanism. Inference: ..."); an invented example.

## Lessons from the Supertraining Chapter 1 review (2026-09-26: 30 FIX, 1 NO-GO of 41)

- **Keep the source's internal contradictions.** When a book says X on one page and not-X on another, record both with their pages and set `contested`. Never pick one side silently. The NO-GO entry reversed the book's SJ-CMJ strength-deficit rule because the book states it both ways.
- **Name the right voice.** In co-authored books, write "the authors" unless a passage clearly belongs to one author. A passage that names Verkhoshansky in the third person is Siff writing.
- **Keep `proven` rare and scoped.** Scope it to the replicated core (for example, "Hill's force-velocity curve"), never the whole entry, and mark any disputed sentence inside it. Four of eight `proven` ratings were lowered.
- **No mechanism the source does not give.** About a dozen "Why it works" sections supplied physiology the book never states. Label it "Inference:" or leave it out.
- **Do not add "well established" or "modern research shows" without a citation.** Name the paper, or delete the phrase.

## Lessons from the 2026-09-27 review wave (Supertraining Ch2-3, Issurin Ch3, Bondarchuk, Evans, Old Bull)

- **Invented Examples are the most common failure.** 34 of 36 Supertraining Ch2-3a Examples were unlabelled inventions. Use the source's own example where it gives one; otherwise start the Example with "Inference:".
- **"Verified against the page image" means you opened the image.** Four Issurin Ch3 entries claimed it for figures they had misread (Fig 3.7 inverted, a Table 3.7 row swapped). Sparse slides are not "bare diagrams" until you have looked.
- **Name the population and method the source gives.** Bondarchuk's data are 7,000+ native and foreign athletes, questionnaires, r >= 0.349, steroid-free; entries that said "Soviet athletes" were wrong everywhere.
- **Check what a cited paper actually says.** Issurin 2016's critique targets Verkhoshansky's concentrated-unidirectional model, not Issurin's A-T-R; Herzog & Leonard 2000 shows force enhancement, against the book's sentence. When the book misreports a study, record both.
- **No review history in entries.** "Prior version", "corrected from a NO-GO finding" and similar belong in `staging/fixes_*_applied.md`, never in the entry body.
- **Fix logs must match the files.** One fixer log claimed fixes that were not made. Fixers run their own grep checks and paste the output.
- **Section headers use the vault form** `**What it is** —` (with the em dash). Do not add suffixes such as ": mandatory". Em dashes are banned only in titles and body text. Never wrap a `[[wikilink]]` across lines.

## Evidence

- Every number, definition and quote carries a checkable locator: PDF page (and printed page if it differs), or file plus timestamp. Never write "confirmed in PDF" unless you opened that page.
- Never invent a number. Keep ambiguity visible: mark unclear audio or OCR as unclear, and do not harmonize two conflicting numbers from the source; record both with their locators.
- OCR sources (`staging/ocr/*.md`): pages listed as low_confidence in the header must be checked against the page image before any number from them is cited. Use the Read tool on the PDF page, or render it.
- **OCR confidence scores miss the worst errors** (checked 2026-09-27). Zatsiorsky 2e: the OCR interleaves the two columns and the sidebars line by line, so its text is not readable prose; use it only to find content, and read and quote from the page image. *CFTS*: single-column prose that mostly reads in order, but upside-down lines come out as gibberish, some lines are dropped, and figures are scrambled, all at "0 low-confidence pages". For any OCR source, quote only after checking the page image, and read every figure and table from the image.

## Confidence

- Practitioner courses and lectures: ceiling `supported`.
- Books: `proven` only for established, widely replicated physiology or mechanics. Soviet-era or single-lab empirical findings and training prescriptions: `supported` at most. `untested` for single cases and anecdotes. `contested` where another library source or modern evidence disagrees (say which).

## Dedup and converge

Before each entry, grep `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library` and the staging library (`C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\staging\library`) for the concept. If it is covered, add a new entry only for a genuinely new angle, and link the existing one in Related. List reciprocal-link suggestions in your final report. Never edit files in the vault or another agent's staging folder.

## Baylor context

Read `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\docs\method-baseline.md` (approved). Use it in When to apply, labelled "Eric's baseline:". Department names: Athletic Performance, Athletic Medicine, Applied Performance. Plain style, no em dashes. Use commas, colons and parentheses.

## Scope and output

- Write ONLY into your assigned staging folder. No git, no vault edits.
- Stop at a chapter or unit boundary. It is better to finish fewer chapters well; the `_book.md` checkpoint lets the next batch resume.
- Final reply: entries by kind and by confidence; chapters or units done and pending with page ranges; reciprocal-link suggestions; unclear or contradictory spots in the source; anything you could not read.

     3	
     4	- Force plates (CMJ testing) were already the department's longitudinal performance-tracking tool well before the 2022-23 wellness-survey experiment, and remained in place after that experiment ended. **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]

    14	# Many Sets and Reps of Plyometrics Do Not Build Fatigue Resistance for Repeated Rebounding; Movement Efficiency Does (Nicol et al, 1997)
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Stated twice in 5.2.4:
    17	- "Many repetitions of plyometric drills frequently are prescribed for some sports because of assumptions that this sort of training will improve fatigue resistance in repeated actions such as rebounding in basketball, yet research has shown this to be untrue (Nicol et al, 1997)" (PDF p. 280 / printed p. 269, verified against the page image).
    18	- "The use of many repetitions and sets of plyometric drills in an attempt to facilitate adaptation to cope with exhaustive bouts of stretch-shortening activities such as rebounding in basketball is not supported by research (Nicol et al, 1997). Instead any improvement in such situations is better mediated by the use of training to enhance movement efficiency. This is a very important point which concerns all explosive and ballistic activities: it is futile to rely predominantly on plyometric drills to enhance sport specific explosive strength and power, because efficiency of motor control is fundamental to all skilled sporting performance" (PDF pp. 288-289 / printed pp. 277-278, verified against the page images).
    19	
    20	**Internal conflict, recorded:** the "futile to rely predominantly" sentence is followed on PDF p. 289 / printed p. 278 by "plyometrics should be the main method in the training of highly qualified athletes for developing explosive strength and reactive ability." See [[heuristic--brief-maximal-tension-vs-plyometrics-by-resistance-size]].
    21	
    22	**Why it works** — The text's stated reason is "efficiency of motor control is fundamental to all skilled sporting performance." It does not describe the Nicol et al (1997) study design or measures, and the paper was not checked for this entry, so what it measured is unverified here.
    23	
    24	**When to apply** — When someone proposes high-rep plyometric circuits to make athletes "fresher" in the fourth quarter. Eric's baseline: "Everything we do is some form of conditioning" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 122). Inference: the text's alternative for repeat-effort tolerance is better movement efficiency in the sport skill itself, not more drill volume; the book also allows "much shorter intervals with submaximal plyometrics to develop explosive-strength endurance" (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274, item 6), so submaximal plyometric endurance work is not ruled out.
    25	
    26	**When NOT to apply** — Not evidence against plyometrics for explosive strength; the same section calls the shock method's training effect "very large." The claim rests on one citation the book does not describe.
    27	
    28	**Example** — The text's own: basketball rebounding as the repeated stretch-shortening task that high plyometric volume was assumed, wrongly, to prepare (PDF p. 280 / printed p. 269).
    29	
    30	**Related** — [[heuristic--maximal-plyometric-and-depth-jump-volume-and-rest]]; [[claim--plyometric-injury-risk-comes-from-prescription-not-the-method]]; [[heuristic--brief-maximal-tension-vs-plyometrics-by-resistance-size]]; [[claim--exercise-economy-improves-with-skill-and-interval-style-costs-more]]

    14	# Plyometric Surfaces and Footwear: Not Too Soft for Rebounds, Yet Sand and Soft Mats Have Their Uses; Swings and Pogo Sticks as Cheap Powermetric Tools
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Surface and apparatus statements in 5.2.4:
    17	- "Footwear or the floor covering should not be very soft or excessively shock absorbent, since this may impair ankle stability, diminish the storage of elastic energy in the SEC (e.g. tendons) and delay the triggering of the positive supportive reaction of the foot (see 6.1.2) when contacting the floor" (PDF p. 284 / printed p. 273, verified against the page image).
    18	- The surface "can also have a significant effect on the outcome of the exercise, as alluded to earlier in comments made about the alterations in motor skill and proprioceptive sensitivity associated with the use of soft-soled shoes and very resilient jumping surfaces. A little known finding is that plyometric and jumping drills performed according to carefully planned progressive patterns in sand can significantly enhance jumping skills in a short period, even as short as 5 days in duration (Montagni & Cardinale, 1996)" (PDF p. 289 / printed p. 278, verified against the page image).
    19	- For depth landings: Dursenev and Raevsky used "soft gymnastic mats", and the authors advise landing "on suitably firm shock-absorbing surfaces" (PDF p. 288 / printed p. 277, verified against the page image).
    20	- Simple apparatus: a children's swing near a wall, where the feet push off the wall after swinging from "a suitable height", progressed by raising the backswing; longer ropes give a slower repetition rate; uprights in front allow upper-body rebounds. The "Pogo-Stick", with intensity "determined by the height of rebound", and boxers' skipping are also offered as "powermetric" tools (PDF p. 289 / printed p. 278, verified against the page image).
    21	
    22	**Internal tension, recorded:** p. 273 warns against very soft, shock-absorbent surfaces for plyometrics, while p. 278 reports fast jumping-skill gains from progressive drills in sand, and p. 277 pairs a soft-mat landing study with advice to land on "suitably firm shock-absorbing surfaces." The book does not reconcile these. Inference: they may refer to different aims (sand for skill and lower impact; firm surfaces for maximal shock rebounds), but the book does not say so.
    23	
    24	**Why it works** — The p. 273 reasons are stated (ankle stability, SEC elastic storage, the foot's positive supportive reaction). No mechanism is given for the sand result. The swing physics is stated by the authors as rope length setting the oscillation time.
    25	
    26	**When to apply** — Choosing where to run maximal rebound work: a firm, not very soft surface and non-cushioned footwear, per p. 273. Inference: sand is an option for early-phase or high-volume submaximal jumping, consistent with the p. 278 finding, but not for maximal depth jumps.
    27	
    28	**When NOT to apply** — The Montagni & Cardinale (1996) result is cited without design or measures; "jumping skills" is not defined. The swing and pogo stick suggestions are the text's ideas, with no data.
    29	
    30	**Example** — The text's own: beach volleyball and beach handball as examples of the value of sand training (PDF p. 289 / printed p. 278).
    31	
    32	**Related** — [[heuristic--depth-jump-execution-cues-landing-gaze-breath]]; [[claim--depth-landings-from-2-to-3-2-m-produce-forces-over-20-times-bodyweight]]; [[heuristic--resisted-and-water-plyometrics]]

    14	# Strength-Endurance: 25-50% 1RM at 60-120 Reps per Minute, Ideally to Fatigue; Above 75-80% 1RM Trains Strength Instead (but the Book Also Prescribes 80-85%)
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Section 5.2.5 (PDF pp. 296-298 / printed pp. 285-287; pp. 296-298 verified against the page images):
    17	- **Eight determinants.** Training for strength-endurance "is determined predominantly by: 1. The magnitude of the load 2. The tempo of movement 3. The duration of each movement and each phase of the movements 4. The rest interval between training sessions 5. The length of the training period 6. The initial levels of strength-endurance of the athlete 7. The kinesiological structure of the movement 8. The relative involvement of static and dynamic strength-endurance" (PDF p. 296 / printed p. 285).
    18	- **Basic prescription.** "Repetition work with weights 25-50% of 1RM at a moderate tempo (from 60-120 repetitions/minute) is used for developing strength-endurance. The effectiveness ... will be higher if the work is executed to complete fatigue, although work of shorter duration (60% of the maximal work capacity time) also will yield satisfactory results (Agolinsky, 1953; Korobkov, 1953; Monogarov, 1958; Diachkov, 1961)" (same page).
    19	- **Ceiling.** "When the activity involves repetitively overcoming significant resistance (exceeding 75-80% of 1RM), one cannot enhance endurance, since one becomes constrained to developing strength predominantly (Zatsiorsky, 1966)" (same page).
    20	- **Progression.** "It is necessary to increase the amount of weight and the number of repetitions as strength-endurance increases" (PDF p. 297 / printed p. 286).
    21	- **Summary rule.** "multiple repetition exercises with various weights should be considered the fundamental method for developing strength-endurance, with the load being determined by the dynamics of the given exercise. In cases requiring intense effort, an optimally heavy weight should be used together with light weights or with exercises simulating the given sport activity. If the special exercise is associated with the prolonged production of moderate force, then it is useful to work with light weights in repeated sets to the point of fatigue or failure" (PDF p. 298 / printed p. 287).
    22	
    23	**Internal conflict, recorded:** the 75-80% ceiling (PDF p. 296 / printed p. 285) conflicts with the sport examples a page later: "Exercises with heavy weights (80-85% of 1RM) ... are recommended for developing strength-endurance in skaters", 4-12 reps per set to complete fatigue with 2-4 min rest (Mikhailov & Panov, 1975), and "Male rowers obtain good results with weights of 50-80% of 1RM" (Ulrich et al, 1966) (PDF p. 297 / printed p. 286). The summary rule on p. 287 ("an optimally heavy weight ... together with light weights" where intense effort is needed) sits closer to the examples than to the ceiling. The book does not reconcile them.
    24	
    25	**Why it works** — The ceiling's stated reason: above 75-80% the work is "constrained to developing strength predominantly." The load-to-fatigue advantage is reported from the cited Soviet studies, without a stated mechanism.
    26	
    27	**When to apply** — Inference: for football, where strength-endurance means repeated forceful efforts (blocking, pushing a sled), the summary rule fits better than the 25-50% band: a heavy-enough load mixed with lighter or sport-simulating work. The 60-120 reps per minute tempo describes cyclic-sport endurance work more than gridiron work. Eric's baseline: for football the priority stack is alactic and aerobic capacity and power, with glycolytic conditioning treated as a "worst case scenario" absorbed through camp and practice (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 116). Inference: to-fatigue strength-endurance sets would add glycolytic load the department deliberately does not program.
    28	
    29	**When NOT to apply** — Do not quote the 75-80% ceiling as a firm rule without the 80-85% skater and 50-80% rower examples. The determinants list has no weightings. "60% of the maximal work capacity time" is not defined further (Inference: 60% of the time to failure is the plain reading).
    30	
    31	**Example** — The authors' own: 25-50% 1RM at 60-120 reps per minute to fatigue, or to 60% of the maximal work time (PDF p. 296 / printed p. 285).
    32

    14	# Large Resistance Calls for the Brief Maximal Tension Method, Small Resistance and Reactive Demand Call for Plyometrics; the Book Disagrees With Itself on Whether Plyometrics Should Be the Main Method
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors' method-selection rules (PDF p. 289 / printed p. 278, verified against the page image unless marked):
    17	- "In those cases where explosive force is associated with the overcoming of large resistance, preference should be given to the brief maximal tension method, as used commonly in Olympic weightlifting. In situations where the resistance is small and the working effect depends upon the reactive ability of the muscles, plyometric methods should be given preference."
    18	- Staging: "Although it should form an integral part of the training programme, plyometrics should not be combined in the beginning stages with resistance exercises such as the brief maximal tension method." "In subsequent stages, plyometrics should be the main method in the training of highly qualified athletes for developing explosive strength and reactive ability."
    19	- Concentric explosive work: "exercises with maximum effort and mixed regimes using weights equal to 40% of 1RM, or 30% of 1RM (Verkhoshansky, 1963; Papysheva, 1966). Explosive-isometric tension up to 80% of maximum should be used in conjunction with this routine."
    20	- In combined sessions, resistance work goes first: combined programmes beat plyometrics alone "provided the resistance movements precede the plyometric activities in individual sessions" (PDF p. 288 / printed p. 277).
    21	- Testing decides: "To ascertain whether an athlete needs plyometric or heavy resistance training depends on measuring the *strength deficit* ... Without such testing, prescription of plyometric training tends to remain hit-and-miss" (PDF p. 284 / printed p. 273; repeated at PDF p. 293 / printed p. 282 in a grammatically broken sentence).
    22	
    23	**Internal conflict, recorded:** "plyometrics should be the main method in the training of highly qualified athletes" (PDF p. 289 / printed p. 278) against, half a page earlier, "it is futile to rely predominantly on plyometric drills to enhance sport specific explosive strength and power, because efficiency of motor control is fundamental to all skilled sporting performance" (PDF pp. 288-289 / printed pp. 277-278). The second follows a Nicol et al (1997) citation. Inference: the first reads like the original shock-method programme and the second like a later addition, but the book marks neither passage by author. The book does not reconcile them.
    24	
    25	**Why it works** — The authors tie each method to the force demand: heavy brief tension for large resistance, reactive shock loading for small resistance. The strength deficit decides which an individual needs (Ch1; see [[heuristic--strength-deficit-sets-training-method-choice]], which records that the book also states the deficit rule two ways).
    26	
    27	**When to apply** — Eric's baseline: "we incorporate the countermovement jump and the isometric mid-thigh pull to get a dynamic strength index, to determine whether we need more plyometric training or more max-strength training" (Eric, interview 2026-09-28, Q21; `docs/method-baseline.md` line 76). Inference: DSI plays the role the authors give the strength deficit (both compare a fast expression of force with a maximal one to choose plyometric versus heavy work), but they are different measures; Eric's baseline Tension 17 records that the DSI cutoffs were never validated and that IMTP peak force drives most of the ratio (line 261). Inference: for linemen, whose sport force is against large resistance, the authors' rule favours brief maximal tension; for skill positions, whose force is against bodymass, it favours plyometrics.
    28	
    29	**When NOT to apply** — Do not cite Supertraining as saying plyometrics should be the main method without the "futile to rely predominantly" sentence, or the reverse. "Beginning stages" and "highly qualified" are not defined. The 40% and 30% of 1RM loads and the 80% explosive-isometric tension are given without sets, reps or rest.
    30	
    31	**Example** — The authors' own contrast: Olympic weightlifting (large resistance, brief maximal tension) versus jumping from depth (small resistance, reactive ability) (PDF p. 289 / printed p. 278).

    14	# Jumpers Doing 475 Depth Jumps in 12 Weeks Gained More Reactive Ability Than a Group Doing 1472 Barbell Push-Offs and 93 Tonnes
    15	
    16	**What it is** — "The plyometric method of developing explosive strength and reactive ability solves to a significant degree the problem of economising training, since it ensures that a high level of special conditioning is attained in the minimum time. Thus, a comparative experiment revealed that a group of track-and-field jumpers executing primarily depth-jumps (all of them did 475 jumps) over a 12 week period in the preparation phase showed greater improvement in reactive ability than the group which trained with traditional methods and executed 1472 general push-offs (squats, jumping and hopping with a barbell weighing 90-95%, 70-80% and 30-40% of 1RM) and lifted a total volume of 93 tons!" (PDF p. 288 / printed p. 277, verified against the page image).
    17	
    18	Two sentences around it: "The training effect of depth-jumps or shock-loading for developing explosive strength is very large, having little equal when compared with the other means of strength training, especially when combined in a complex with other forms of intensive strength training", corroborated by Semyenov 1971, Tatyan 1974, Dobrovolsky 1972, Savin 1974, Khodykin 1974 and Deniskin 1976 (same page). And: "Carefully periodised training programmes which combine resistance exercises with plyometrics can develop explosive strength even more effectively than plyometrics alone, provided the resistance movements precede the plyometric activities in individual sessions" (same page).
    19	
    20	**Why it works** — The authors give the result as evidence of "economising training"; no mechanism is stated here beyond the shock-method rationale elsewhere in 5.2.4.
    21	
    22	**When to apply** — Making the case to coaches that a small, well-placed depth-jump dose can do more for reactive ability than a large barbell volume. Inference: the companion sentence (resistance work before plyometrics in the same session) is a direct sequencing rule for combined sessions.

    14	# Set Depth-Jump Height by Strength Fitness: Too High Once the Transition Slows or the Heels Are Driven to the Ground; Raise Speed Before Height
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors' rules for choosing drop height in training (all on pages verified against the page image):
    17	- "The optimal depth of the jump is determined by the athlete's strength fitness, while the athlete should ensure that significant dynamic force is developed without slowing down the transition from eccentric to concentric work by the muscles involved" (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274).
    18	- "The optimal height of a depth jump does not result in a landing where the heel is forced to the ground by momentum" (PDF p. 287 / printed p. 276, item 8).
    19	- "One should aim to increase the speed and acceleration of movement before increasing the drop height or take-off height" (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274, item 5).
    20	- "One should begin at a relatively low height and increase it gradually to the optimal height. It makes sense to begin by jumping upward and forward and only after sufficient training, to jump strictly upward" (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275, item 1).
    21	- Height is preferred over added weight, and a force plate can find the height for a required force (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274, item 1).
    22	- For jumping power "one can work without an additional load and utilise only falling bodymass" (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274). Fig 5.10 (Verkhoshansky, 1977) shows three variants: two under "Horizontal Projection" (after the drop, the athlete rebounds forward over low objects drawn on the ground) and one under "Vertical Projection" (rebound upward toward a hanging marker) (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275, read from the image; the drawings are small, so the object details are approximate).
    23	
    24	**Why it works** — The authors' reason is the transition: height is only useful while it raises dynamic force without "slowing down the transition from eccentric to concentric work". Heels forced to the ground is their visible sign that momentum has overwhelmed the athlete. Inference: a heel strike means the ankle has been driven through its range, which lengthens the amortisation the authors want kept short; the book states only the rule.
    25	
    26	**When to apply** — Inference: with a force plate or contact mat, find each athlete's height by stepping the box up until contact time rises or rebound height falls, and stop below that point; on the field, watch for heels hitting the ground. This individual approach is consistent with the authors' "determined by the athlete's strength fitness." Eric's baseline: the department reads reactive ability through mRSI, which "was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 74). Inference: a drop-jump RSI (jump height over contact time) taken at stepped heights is the direct test of the authors' "without slowing down the transition" rule, but Eric's baseline names CMJ-based mRSI, not drop jumps.
    27	
    28	**When NOT to apply** — The Ch4.2.3 figures put the optimum for advanced jumpers at 0.75-1.15 m ([[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]]); the rules here give no number, and the authors stress starting "considerably lower" for anyone unused to the training. The heel rule is a coaching sign, not a measured threshold. Upward-and-forward before strictly upward is the authors' order; they give no reason.

    19	3. **Amortisation phase:** the KE "produces a powerful myotatic stretch reflex which leads to eccentric muscle contraction accompanied by explosive isometric contraction" and stretching of the SEC (e.g. tendons).     20	4. **Rebound phase:** release of elastic energy from the SEC, with involuntary concentric contraction evoked by the stretch reflex, "as well as possible local change in the muscle fibre mechanics"; it "may include the contribution added by voluntary concentric contraction."

    16	**What it is** — The authors replace the "classically plyometric or not" argument with a classification (PDF pp. 283-284 / printed pp. 272-273; Fig 5.8 verified against the page image):
    17	- **Impact versus non-impact.** In impact plyometrics "the rebound is stimulated by contact with a surface or object"; in non-impact plyometrics the recoil "is mediated by explosive eccentric action of the muscles that produce a movement not terminated by contact with a surface." Depth jumps are impact; "snap kicks or rapidly-retracted blows in boxing or the martial arts" are non-impact, which "may also be maximal or submaximal."
    18	- **Maximal, submaximal, non-plyometric.** *Maximal plyometrics* are "low-repetition activities where the intensity of the depth jump or rebound exercise is such that maximal or near-maximal rebound tension is produced." *Sub-maximal plyometrics* "do not produce maximal muscular tension, although they are still performed with a minimally long contact phase": "lower box heights are used for depth jumps and the athlete does not strive to reach maximal rebound height"; "rapid double-footed bouncing or low skipping on the spot" are other examples.     17	- **Impact versus non-impact.** In impact plyometrics "the rebound is stimulated by contact with a surface or object"; in non-impact plyometrics the recoil "is mediated by explosive eccentric action of the muscles that produce a movement not terminated by contact with a surface." Depth jumps are impact; "snap kicks or rapidly-retracted blows in boxing or the martial arts" are non-impact, which "may also be maximal or submaximal."
    18	- **Maximal, submaximal, non-plyometric.** *Maximal plyometrics* are "low-repetition activities where the intensity of the depth jump or rebound exercise is such that maximal or near-maximal rebound tension is produced." *Sub-maximal plyometrics* "do not produce maximal muscular tension, although they are still performed with a minimally long contact phase": "lower box heights are used for depth jumps and the athlete does not strive to reach maximal rebound height"; "rapid double-footed bouncing or low skipping on the spot" are other examples. The three are drawn in one box "as a reminder that there is really a continuum of intensities."
    19	- **Classical, supplementary, preparatory.** Classical plyometric exercises are *functional* ("matched as closely as possible to the specific explosive actions of the particular sport with respect to movement pattern, muscle involvement, timing and direction of motion") or *non-functional* ("general training of the explosive qualities"). Functional examples: forward bounding for long jump, backward rebounds for shot put, one-legged forward hopping for jumping, and for basketball "both short and relatively long amortisation phases in vertical rebounds." Preparatory or supplementary drills are weight training for muscular strength ("especially eccentric strength") and connective tissue, plus jumping, swinging, throwing and catching drills "with longer duration transition phases"; "Most of the drills described in popular books on plyometrics in the West are actually supplementary exercises."
    20	- **Pseudo-plyometrics.** Drills "incorrectly labelled as plyometric because they include a sudden stop or some form of jump", e.g. "'power moves' (involving quick landings and delayed jumps in a semi-squat position)" and many "'water plyos'" in aerobics classes; lacking "an explosive rebound phase with a short coupling time", they serve as "preparatory non-plyometrics."
    21	
    22	Fig 5.8 as drawn: Plyometric training splits into impact and non-impact; below these sit maximal plyometrics, submaximal plyometrics and non-plyometrics; under maximal sits "classical plyometrics" (split into functional and non-functional); under submaximal sits "supplementary plyometrics"; under non-plyometrics sits "preparatory/supplementary activities" (split into weight training and "jumps throws etc"). The text lists classical, supplementary and preparatory as three flat categories; the figure ties each to one intensity level.
    23	
    24	**Why it works** — The authors' reason for classifying rather than arguing definitions: the definitional debate "becomes complex and academic, with no real benefit to the prescription of plyometric training" (PDF p. 283 / printed p. 272). Intensity is graded by the momentum at contact (see [[heuristic--rate-plyometric-intensity-by-contact-momentum-from-drop-height]]).
    25	
    26	**When to apply** — Labelling every jump, bound, hop and med-ball drill in a plan by class, so volume and rest rules are applied to the right class: the authors' low-rep, long-rest rules are for maximal plyometrics, while submaximal and preparatory drills tolerate more volume (see [[heuristic--maximal-plyometric-and-depth-jump-volume-and-rest]]). Inference: in football, a vertical depth jump is classical non-functional, while a bound or single-leg hop that matches a cut or drive phase in direction and timing would be the authors' "functional" class.
    27	
    28	**When NOT to apply** — The text and figure place "supplementary" differently (a flat list of three versus a level under submaximal; and "preparatory or supplementary drills" in the text against "supplementary plyometrics" as its own box in the figure). The class boundaries are a continuum by the authors' own statement, so the labels are not sharp cut-offs.
    29	
    30	**Example** — The authors' own: depth jumps (impact, maximal when performed for maximal rebound), low box depth jumps without striving for height (submaximal), karate snap kicks (non-impact), "power moves" in aerobics (pseudo-plyometric).
    31

    13	
    14	# Grade Plyometric Intensity by Momentum at Contact (Set by Drop Height), Since a 1RM Does Not Exist; Prefer Height Over Added Weight
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors propose "a *powermetrics intensity scale* similar to that used in weightlifting, where exercises are ranked in terms of percentages of one's 1RM." Because "the concept of 1RMs is meaningless in plyometric training", one must use estimates of muscle tension or of "the impulse ... produced during the contact phase". "Impulse is equivalent to the change of momentum (m.ΔV) during the amortisation phase, so that its magnitude for a falling body depends on the height from which the body drops. Thus, the momentum just before contact (estimated from height of the drop jump or distance fallen by the object) may serve as a measure of intensity." At the top of the scale is maximal plyometrics, "the equivalent of the emotionally demanding competitive maximum, CFmax"; at the bottom, preparatory non-impact plyometrics (PDF p. 283 / printed p. 272, verified against the page image).
    17	
    18	The prescription list adds: "The magnitude of the impulsive load is determined by the weight and the height of its free-fall. The optimal combination is determined empirically in each specific case; however, preference should be given to a large height over a heavy weight. Since the resulting force is governed by Newton's Second Law (F = m.a), a force plate may be used to determine the height of drop to produce the required force" (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274, item 1, verified against the page image). Item 4 says rep dosage can be set more precisely "to calculate the force involved (from bodymass and the drop height) and the athlete's level of special speed-strength" (same page).
    19	
    20	**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning is the impulse-momentum statement quoted. Inference (physics): for a body falling from rest through height h, speed at contact is √(2gh), so momentum at contact is m·√(2gh). Momentum therefore rises with the square root of drop height, not in proportion to it: doubling the drop height raises contact momentum by a factor of √2, about 41%, and quadrupling it doubles momentum. Inference (physics): the peak force on landing is not fixed by drop height alone; for the same momentum, a shorter, stiffer arrest gives a higher average force (average net force = change in momentum divided by contact time). That is why the authors' force plate step is needed to find the height that gives a target force.
    21	
    22	**When to apply** — Progressing depth jumps or rebounds: rank drills by drop height and bodymass rather than counting all "plyos" as equal, and raise height before adding external load. Inference: with ForceDecks, a drop jump from a known box gives landing force and contact time for each athlete, which is the measurement the authors' item 1 asks for.
    23	
    24	**When NOT to apply** — Momentum at contact is an intensity proxy for impact drills with a fall; it does not grade non-impact or ground-based bounding drills where there is no measured drop. The authors give no numeric scale bands (no "% of CFmax" per height). Item 1's "F = m.a" sentence does not on its own let you compute landing force from height (see the Inference above). Height also has an upper limit: past the optimum the transition slows (see [[heuristic--depth-jump-height-set-by-transition-speed-and-heel-contact]] and [[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]]).
    25	
    26	**Example** — Inference: a 100 kg athlete stepping off a 0.5 m box lands at about √(2 × 9.81 × 0.5) ≈ 3.1 m/s, about 313 kg·m/s of momentum; from a 1.0 m box about 4.4 m/s and about 443 kg·m/s, roughly 41% more, not double. This calculation is not in the source.
    27	
    28	**Related** — [[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]] (Ch4.2.3, the 0.75-1.15 m range); [[framework--kinetic-energy-stimulation-mechanical-basis-and-advantages]]; [[claim--thrown-load-height-decreases-with-load-increases-with-drop-height]] (Ch4.2.3, heavier loads not beneficial); [[framework--plyometric-training-classification-impact-intensity-and-function]]; [[heuristic--rfd-as-correspondence-criterion-and-impulse-cannot-compare-movements]]

    13	
    14	# The Lewis Formula P = 21.693 x B x √H Tracks Jump Progress, but It Computes a Falling-Body Power, Not Take-Off Power
    15	
    16	**What it is** — In the preparatory programme, the authors suggest tracking jump progress this way: "To gain an idea of individual progress, the power developed may be calculated from the Lewis nomogram or from the formula: Power P = (21.693) B√H watts, where B = bodymass in kg and H = height jumped in metres" (PDF p. 288 / printed p. 277, formula read from the page image; the text layer garbles it as "b Vh").
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The book gives no derivation. Inference (physics): 21.693 = 9.8 × √4.9, so the formula is P = B·g·√(g·H/2) with g = 9.8 m/s². A body falling freely from rest through height H reaches √(2gH); its mean speed during the fall is half that, √(gH/2). So the formula is body weight (B·g) times the mean speed of a body falling through H, in watts. It is a fixed function of bodymass and jump height only.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — As the authors use it: a cheap way to see whether an individual's bodymass-scaled jump is improving over time, when only a jump height and a scale are available. Eric's baseline: jumps are tested on ForceDecks force plates (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 77, the CMJ family protocol). Inference: where force plates are available, measured propulsive power replaces this estimate; the formula is only a fallback.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — Inference: because the formula is weight times the mean speed of a free fall through H, it is not the athlete's peak or mean propulsive power during take-off, which depends on how fast force is produced over the push-off distance; two athletes with the same mass and jump height get the same value even if one pushes off much faster. Do not compare its values with force-plate peak power. The book gives no validation data for it.
    23	
    24	**Example** — Inference: a 100 kg athlete jumping 0.50 m gives P = 21.693 × 100 × √0.50 ≈ 1,534 W; at 0.55 m, ≈ 1,609 W. This arithmetic is not in the source.
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[heuristic--preparatory-progression-before-depth-jumps]]; [[claim--average-or-peak-force-times-velocity-is-not-power]] (Ch4.3, the authors' own warning about crude power estimates); [[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]]

    12	---
    13	
    14	# Plyometric Injury Risk Comes From Prescription (Overload and Overuse), Not the Method; Regularly Impact-Loaded Cartilage Is Reported as Healthier
    15	
    16	**What it is** — In "Plyometric Training and Safety" (PDF pp. 280-281 / printed pp. 269-270; p. 280 verified against the page image) the text argues:
    17	- The claim that "plyometric drills on their own are dangerous and useless has not been proved experimentally or clinically"; the danger is "inferred from the magnitude of the impulsive peak forces which have been measured via force plate research", and an experiment isolating plyometric effects with matched controls "is very difficult to design."
    18	- Opponents imply running and jumping "in the context of normal sport are perfectly safe, but in the context of special plyometric drills are dangerous", and assume joints do not follow SAID (Specific Adaptation to Imposed Demands).
    19	- Cartilage: "joints subjected to heavy impact are relatively free from osteoarthritis in old age and ... those subjected to much lower loading experience a greater incidence of osteoarthritis and cartilage fibrillation (Bullough et al, 1973; Kempson et al, 1975; Seedhom & Swann, 1985; Seedhom & Wright, 1988; Seedhom et al, 1977)." Siff's former colleague Mark Swanepoel (University of the Witwatersrand) noted that fibrillation at any age increases going up from ankle to knee, hip and lumbar spine. Regularly impulse-loaded cartilage is "mechanically much stiffer", while cartilage "heavily loaded infrequently softens due to decrease in proteoglycan production" (Swanepoel, 1998).
    20	- "it is not the inherent nature of plyometrics which may produce injury, but the manner in which it is used." Western practice earns much of the criticism: "encyclopaedic compilations of drills offered in extended, isolated and highly repetitive forms"; drills often prescribed without regard to "loading imposed by other work or play ... or the use of formal restoration"; and "the athlete's sport alone may offer all or most of the plyometric training that is necessary."
    21	- "overtraining comprises two distinct components: overload (the imposition of too great a force at any given time) and overuse (the imposition of too great a volume of exercise)." An "individually appropriate volume and intensity (e.g. via choice of drop height)" with "gradual progressive overload" and "adequate restoration regimes need pose no greater risks than the naturally occurring plyometric actions found in running or jumping" (PDF pp. 280-281).
    22	
    23	Voice: Siff (the passage names "Siff's former colleague").
    24	
    25	**Why it works** — The stated mechanism is adaptation (SAID) and the cartilage findings cited. Inference: overload maps to drop height and rebound effort, overuse to contacts per session and week, which gives two separate dials to manage.
    26	
    27	**When to apply** — Answering "are depth jumps dangerous?" for coaches or medical staff: the text's position is that risk is a dose question. Inference: in football, count the plyometric loading already present in practice (cutting, jumping, sprinting) before adding drills, as the text's "sport alone may offer all or most" warning suggests.
    28	
    29	**When NOT to apply** — The text argues mainly from absence of proof and from cartilage studies of everyday joint loading; it cites no controlled study showing plyometric drills are safe. The "heavy impact joints are free from osteoarthritis" sentence compares joints and loading histories, not plyometric training programs, so do not cite it as evidence that depth jumps protect joints. The cited studies were not checked for this entry.
    30	
    31	**Example** — The text's own: the Nicol et al (1997) finding, that many repetitions do not improve fatigue resistance in basketball rebounding, as an example of a Western volume habit that is "untrue" (PDF p. 280 / printed p. 269; see [[claim--high-volume-plyometrics-do-not-build-rebound-fatigue-resistance]]).
    32	
    33	**Related** — [[claim--collagen-loading-curve-and-injury-risk]]; [[claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]]; [[heuristic--maximal-plyometric-and-depth-jump-volume-and-rest]]; [[claim--squat-1-5-to-2-bodymass-rule-applies-to-maximal-depth-jumps-only]]

    13	
    14	# Resisted Plyometrics Only Occasionally and Never With Heavy Weights or Stiff Cords in Depth Jumps; Water Plyometrics Are a Safer Submaximal Option
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Under "Resisted and Water Plyometric Training" (PDF pp. 292-293 / printed pp. 281-282; p. 293 verified against the page image, p. 292 from the text layer):
    17	- Resistance can be imposed in the amortisation phase, the concentric rebound or both: light weights, or "elastic cords attached to a harness located near the waist or hips." Both "increase the landing impact and ostensibly increase the strength of reflex muscle contraction", but "also increase the risk of impact and overload injuries and should be applied occasionally with great caution. Even normal running or hurdling with very light weights constitutes a form of loaded plyometric training."
    18	- Resistance methods "should not use heavy weights or stiff elastic cords during depth jumps, since this increases the coupling time and imposes unnecessarily large loads on the spine and the tendons of the lower extremities, especially during the landing or contact phase."
    19	- Water or "aqua plyometrics" decrease landing force and increase resistance in the recoil. They do "not offer maximal or shock method plyometrics" but serve as preparatory or submaximal plyometrics, "especially for one-legged drills." Water depth sets the resistance: "chest or shoulder high water offering greater resistance during the landing and take-off phases, less intense eccentric muscle activity, smaller impact forces and enhanced safety." Repeated aqua jumps for "rebound explosive muscle endurance" are "considerably safer than their land-based equivalents, though they should not completely replace the latter, since they do not adequately develop the specific neuromuscular patterns or functional needs of explosive sports."
    20	
    21	**Why it works** — The authors' reasons are stated: heavy load lengthens the coupling time (taking the drill out of classical plyometrics) and loads spine and tendons; water reduces impact and eccentric intensity.
    22	
    23	**When to apply** — Inference: aqua jumps suit early return-to-training or single-leg plyometric progressions where impact must be limited, consistent with the authors' "especially for one-legged drills." Light loads during running or hurdling are already loaded plyometrics, per the authors, so they belong in the plyometric count.
    24	
    25	**When NOT to apply** — Not a replacement for land plyometrics for explosive sport (the authors' own limit). "Light" and "heavy" weights and "stiff" cords are not quantified. The "water plyos" in aerobics classes the authors call pseudo-plyometric (PDF p. 284 / printed p. 273) differ from these structured aqua drills; do not conflate them.
    26	
    27	**Example** — The authors' own: chest- or shoulder-high water for one-legged preparatory jumps (PDF p. 293 / printed p. 282).
    28	
    29	**Related** — [[framework--plyometric-training-classification-impact-intensity-and-function]]; [[claim--thrown-load-height-decreases-with-load-increases-with-drop-height]] (Ch4.2.3, heavier loads not beneficial for kinetic-energy work); [[heuristic--plyometric-surface-footwear-and-simple-apparatus]]; [[heuristic--plyometric-training-coupling-under-0-15-s-feedforward-and-force-time-pattern]]

    12	---
    13	
    14	# How Long a Prestretch Helps Varies From About 0.25 s to About 4 s by Task, and the Book's Own Figure Attribution Conflicts
    15	
    16	**What it is** — After stating the about 0.15 s coupling guide, the authors say it "requires some qualification" and list conflicting results (PDF pp. 281-282 / printed pp. 270-271; Figs 5.6 and 5.7 verified against the page image):
    17	- Wilson et al (1990), bench press: "the benefits of prior stretch may endure for as long as 4 seconds, at which stage it is suggested that all stored elastic energy is lost (see Fig 5.6)."
    18	- Chapman and Caldwell (1985), forearm movement: benefits "dissipated within 0.25 second, a figure which agrees with Siff's analysis of explosive rebound elbow flexion without additional loading (Fig 5.7)."
    19	- Wilson et al (1991), rebound action of the chest and arms: "no benefits of prior stretching are evident after 0.37 second."
    20	
    21	Summary in the text: "delays of as long as a second or two can still produce significant augmentation of the subsequent concentric phase for some activities, but delays as short as 0.2 second are sufficient to dissipate the benefits of prior stretch during other activities."
    22	
    23	Figure readings (approximate, from the image). Fig 5.6, "% decay" against delay 0-5 s: rises steeply from 0 near 0.1-0.2 s, roughly half decayed near 1 s, about 80% by 2 s, near 100% at about 4 s. Fig 5.7, unloaded elbow flexion, delay 0.1-0.25 s: close to linear from 0% at 0.1 s to 100% at 0.25 s.
    24	
    25	**Internal conflict, recorded:** the Fig 5.6 caption reads "based on the data of Wilson et al, 1991", but the text gives the 4 s bench-press result to Wilson et al (1990) and the 0.37 s chest/arms result to Wilson et al (1991) (PDF pp. 281-282 / printed pp. 270-271). The curve's near-total decay at about 4 s matches the text's 1990 sentence, not the 0.37 s result. Which year is right is not resolvable from the book.
    26	
    27	The authors' partial resolutions:
    28	- Fibre type (Bosco et al, 1982a): high-FT individuals show the maximum plyometric effect with a short eccentric phase, small range and brief coupling; high-ST individuals jump best with a longer eccentric phase, greater range and longer coupling, "since the actin-myosin cross-bridging attachment time is of greater duration" (PDF p. 282 / printed p. 271).
    29	- Joint-specific maximum delays "probably" exist, but the body has many reflexes acting "at different rates"; tonic (static) and phasic (dynamic) stretch reflexes differ (PDF p. 282 / printed p. 271).
    30	- The weightlifters' "pre-stretch principle" (hold an intense stretch "for a couple of seconds and then thrust") "would seem" to involve the more tonic reflex with longer coupling, and "could certainly not be called plyometric", while phasic reflexes are "more likely" behind classical plyometrics (PDF p. 283 / printed p. 272, verified against the page image).
    31	
    32	**Why it works** — The authors offer fibre type and tonic versus phasic reflexes as explanations, with hedges ("partial solution", "would seem", "more likely"). They do not test either against the conflicting delay data.
    33	
    34	**When to apply** — When someone quotes one fixed "the stretch benefit is gone after X ms" number: the book shows the window depends on the task (unloaded elbow about 0.25 s; loaded bench press up to about 4 s). Inference: for loaded lifts a paused rep still keeps some prestretch benefit for a second or more, per Fig 5.6, while for unloaded fast rebounds the benefit is gone within a few tenths of a second, per Fig 5.7.
    35	
    36	**When NOT to apply** — Do not cite Fig 5.6 under a single Wilson year without noting the caption-text conflict. The figure values are read from small plots and are approximate. Fig 5.7 is Siff's own analysis: the book says it "was derived from some of this work on upper-body non-impact plyometrics", the research "conducted in this field by the author in 1994" (PDF p. 292 / printed p. 281), and gives no subject numbers or publication for it. The fibre-type and reflex explanations are proposals, not demonstrated here.
    37	
    38	**Example** — The authors' own: unloaded explosive elbow flexion loses its prestretch benefit over 0.1-0.25 s (Fig 5.7), while the bench-press benefit decays over about 4 s (Fig 5.6).
    39	
    40	**Related** — [[heuristic--match-plyometric-prescription-to-joint-angle-and-fiber-type]] (Ch1.7, the same Bosco et al 1982 fibre-type finding); [[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]]; [[framework--stretch-reflex-types-and-neuromuscular-control-of-flexibility]]; [[heuristic--plyometric-training-coupling-under-0-15-s-feedforward-and-force-time-pattern]]

Inference (physics): for a body falling from rest through height h, speed at contact is √(2gh), so momentum at contact is m·√(2gh). Momentum therefore rises with the square root of drop height, not in proportion to it: doubling the drop height raises contact momentum by a factor of √2, about 41%, and quadrupling it doubles momentum. Inference (physics): the peak force on landing is not fixed by drop height alone; for the same momentum, a shorter, stiffer arrest gives a higher average force (average net force = change in momentum divided by contact time). That is why the authors' force plate step is needed to find the height that gives a target force.
    21	
    22	**When to apply** — Progressing depth jumps or rebounds: rank drills by drop height and bodymass rather than counting all "plyos" as equal, and raise height before adding external load. Inference: with ForceDecks, a drop jump from a known box gives landing force and contact time for each athlete, which is the measurement the authors' item 1 asks for.
    23	
    24	**When NOT to apply** — Momentum at contact is an intensity proxy for impact drills with a fall; it does not grade non-impact or ground-based bounding drills where there is no measured drop. The authors give no numeric scale bands (no "% of CFmax" per height). Item 1's "F = m.a" sentence does not on its own let you compute landing force from height (see the Inference above). Height also has an upper limit: past the optimum the transition slows (see [[heuristic--depth-jump-height-set-by-transition-speed-and-heel-contact]] and [[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]]).
    25	
    26	**Example** — Inference: a 100 kg athlete stepping off a 0.5 m box lands at about √(2 × 9.81 × 0.5) ≈ 3.1 m/s, about 313 kg·m/s of momentum; from a 1.0 m box about 4.4 m/s and about 443 kg·m/s, roughly 41% more, not double. This calculation is not in the source.
    27	
    28	**Related** — [[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]] (Ch4.2.3, the 0.75-1.15 m range); [[framework--kinetic-energy-stimulation-mechanical-basis-and-advantages]]; [[claim--thrown-load-height-decreases-with-load-increases-with-drop-height]] (Ch4.2.3, heavier loads not beneficial); [[framework--plyometric-training-classification-impact-intensity-and-function]]; [[heuristic--rfd-as-correspondence-criterion-and-impulse-cannot-compare-movements]]

    13	
    14	# The Lewis Formula P = 21.693 x B x √H Tracks Jump Progress, but It Computes a Falling-Body Power, Not Take-Off Power
    15	
    16	**What it is** — In the preparatory programme, the authors suggest tracking jump progress this way: "To gain an idea of individual progress, the power developed may be calculated from the Lewis nomogram or from the formula: Power P = (21.693) B√H watts, where B = bodymass in kg and H = height jumped in metres" (PDF p. 288 / printed p. 277, formula read from the page image; the text layer garbles it as "b Vh").
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The book gives no derivation. Inference (physics): 21.693 = 9.8 × √4.9, so the formula is P = B·g·√(g·H/2) with g = 9.8 m/s². A body falling freely from rest through height H reaches √(2gH); its mean speed during the fall is half that, √(gH/2). So the formula is body weight (B·g) times the mean speed of a body falling through H, in watts. It is a fixed function of bodymass and jump height only.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — As the authors use it: a cheap way to see whether an individual's bodymass-scaled jump is improving over time, when only a jump height and a scale are available. Eric's baseline: jumps are tested on ForceDecks force plates (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 77, the CMJ family protocol). Inference: where force plates are available, measured propulsive power replaces this estimate; the formula is only a fallback.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — Inference: because the formula is weight times the mean speed of a free fall through H, it is not the athlete's peak or mean propulsive power during take-off, which depends on how fast force is produced over the push-off distance; two athletes with the same mass and jump height get the same value even if one pushes off much faster. Do not compare its values with force-plate peak power. The book gives no validation data for it.
    23	
    24	**Example** — Inference: a 100 kg athlete jumping 0.50 m gives P = 21.693 × 100 × √0.50 ≈ 1,534 W; at 0.55 m, ≈ 1,609 W. This arithmetic is not in the source.
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[heuristic--preparatory-progression-before-depth-jumps]]; [[claim--average-or-peak-force-times-velocity-is-not-power]] (Ch4.3, the authors' own warning about crude power estimates); [[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]]

    13	
    14	# Plyometric Injury Risk Comes From Prescription (Overload and Overuse), Not the Method; Regularly Impact-Loaded Cartilage Is Reported as Healthier
    15	
    16	**What it is** — In "Plyometric Training and Safety" (PDF pp. 280-281 / printed pp. 269-270; p. 280 verified against the page image) the text argues:
    17	- The claim that "plyometric drills on their own are dangerous and useless has not been proved experimentally or clinically"; the danger is "inferred from the magnitude of the impulsive peak forces which have been measured via force plate research", and an experiment isolating plyometric effects with matched controls "is very difficult to design."
    18	- Opponents imply running and jumping "in the context of normal sport are perfectly safe, but in the context of special plyometric drills are dangerous", and assume joints do not follow SAID (Specific Adaptation to Imposed Demands).
    19	- Cartilage: "joints subjected to heavy impact are relatively free from osteoarthritis in old age and ... those subjected to much lower loading experience a greater incidence of osteoarthritis and cartilage fibrillation (Bullough et al, 1973; Kempson et al, 1975; Seedhom & Swann, 1985; Seedhom & Wright, 1988; Seedhom et al, 1977)." Siff's former colleague Mark Swanepoel (University of the Witwatersrand) noted that fibrillation at any age increases going up from ankle to knee, hip and lumbar spine. Regularly impulse-loaded cartilage is "mechanically much stiffer", while cartilage "heavily loaded infrequently softens due to decrease in proteoglycan production" (Swanepoel, 1998).
    20	- "it is not the inherent nature of plyometrics which may produce injury, but the manner in which it is used." Western practice earns much of the criticism: "encyclopaedic compilations of drills offered in extended, isolated and highly repetitive forms"; drills often prescribed without regard to "loading imposed by other work or play ... or the use of formal restoration"; and "the athlete's sport alone may offer all or most of the plyometric training that is necessary."
    21	- "overtraining comprises two distinct components: overload (the imposition of too great a force at any given time) and overuse (the imposition of too great a volume of exercise)." An "individually appropriate volume and intensity (e.g. via choice of drop height)" with "gradual progressive overload" and "adequate restoration regimes need pose no greater risks than the naturally occurring plyometric actions found in running or jumping" (PDF pp. 280-281).
    22	
    23	Voice: Siff (the passage names "Siff's former colleague").
    24	
    25	**Why it works** — The stated mechanism is adaptation (SAID) and the cartilage findings cited. Inference: overload maps to drop height and rebound effort, overuse to contacts per session and week, which gives two separate dials to manage.
    26	
    27	**When to apply** — Answering "are depth jumps dangerous?" for coaches or medical staff: the text's position is that risk is a dose question. Inference: in football, count the plyometric loading already present in practice (cutting, jumping, sprinting) before adding drills, as the text's "sport alone may offer all or most" warning suggests.
    28	
    29	**When NOT to apply** — The text argues mainly from absence of proof and from cartilage studies of everyday joint loading; it cites no controlled study showing plyometric drills are safe. The "heavy impact joints are free from osteoarthritis" sentence compares joints and loading histories, not plyometric training programs, so do not cite it as evidence that depth jumps protect joints. The cited studies were not checked for this entry.
    30	
    31	**Example** — The text's own: the Nicol et al (1997) finding, that many repetitions do not improve fatigue resistance in basketball rebounding, as an example of a Western volume habit that is "untrue" (PDF p. 280 / printed p. 269; see [[claim--high-volume-plyometrics-do-not-build-rebound-fatigue-resistance]]).
    32

    14	# Resisted Plyometrics Only Occasionally and Never With Heavy Weights or Stiff Cords in Depth Jumps; Water Plyometrics Are a Safer Submaximal Option
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Under "Resisted and Water Plyometric Training" (PDF pp. 292-293 / printed pp. 281-282; p. 293 verified against the page image, p. 292 from the text layer):
    17	- Resistance can be imposed in the amortisation phase, the concentric rebound or both: light weights, or "elastic cords attached to a harness located near the waist or hips." Both "increase the landing impact and ostensibly increase the strength of reflex muscle contraction", but "also increase the risk of impact and overload injuries and should be applied occasionally with great caution. Even normal running or hurdling with very light weights constitutes a form of loaded plyometric training."
    18	- Resistance methods "should not use heavy weights or stiff elastic cords during depth jumps, since this increases the coupling time and imposes unnecessarily large loads on the spine and the tendons of the lower extremities, especially during the landing or contact phase."
    19	- Water or "aqua plyometrics" decrease landing force and increase resistance in the recoil. They do "not offer maximal or shock method plyometrics" but serve as preparatory or submaximal plyometrics, "especially for one-legged drills." Water depth sets the resistance: "chest or shoulder high water offering greater resistance during the landing and take-off phases, less intense eccentric muscle activity, smaller impact forces and enhanced safety." Repeated aqua jumps for "rebound explosive muscle endurance" are "considerably safer than their land-based equivalents, though they should not completely replace the latter, since they do not adequately develop the specific neuromuscular patterns or functional needs of explosive sports."
    20	
    21	**Why it works** — The authors' reasons are stated: heavy load lengthens the coupling time (taking the drill out of classical plyometrics) and loads spine and tendons; water reduces impact and eccentric intensity.
    22	
    23	**When to apply** — Inference: aqua jumps suit early return-to-training or single-leg plyometric progressions where impact must be limited, consistent with the authors' "especially for one-legged drills." Light loads during running or hurdling are already loaded plyometrics, per the authors, so they belong in the plyometric count.
    24	
    25	**When NOT to apply** — Not a replacement for land plyometrics for explosive sport (the authors' own limit). "Light" and "heavy" weights and "stiff" cords are not quantified. The "water plyos" in aerobics classes the authors call pseudo-plyometric (PDF p. 284 / printed p. 273) differ from these structured aqua drills; do not conflate them.
    26	
    27	**Example** — The authors' own: chest- or shoulder-high water for one-legged preparatory jumps (PDF p. 293 / printed p. 282).
    28	
    29	**Related** — [[framework--plyometric-training-classification-impact-intensity-and-function]]; [[claim--thrown-load-height-decreases-with-load-increases-with-drop-height]] (Ch4.2.3, heavier loads not beneficial for kinetic-energy work); [[heuristic--plyometric-surface-footwear-and-simple-apparatus]]; [[heuristic--plyometric-training-coupling-under-0-15-s-feedforward-and-force-time-pattern]]

    13	
    14	# How Long a Prestretch Helps Varies From About 0.25 s to About 4 s by Task, and the Book's Own Figure Attribution Conflicts
    15	
    16	**What it is** — After stating the about 0.15 s coupling guide, the authors say it "requires some qualification" and list conflicting results (PDF pp. 281-282 / printed pp. 270-271; Figs 5.6 and 5.7 verified against the page image):
    17	- Wilson et al (1990), bench press: "the benefits of prior stretch may endure for as long as 4 seconds, at which stage it is suggested that all stored elastic energy is lost (see Fig 5.6)."
    18	- Chapman and Caldwell (1985), forearm movement: benefits "dissipated within 0.25 second, a figure which agrees with Siff's analysis of explosive rebound elbow flexion without additional loading (Fig 5.7)."
    19	- Wilson et al (1991), rebound action of the chest and arms: "no benefits of prior stretching are evident after 0.37 second."
    20	
    21	Summary in the text: "delays of as long as a second or two can still produce significant augmentation of the subsequent concentric phase for some activities, but delays as short as 0.2 second are sufficient to dissipate the benefits of prior stretch during other activities."
    22	
    23	Figure readings (approximate, from the image). Fig 5.6, "% decay" against delay 0-5 s: rises steeply from 0 near 0.1-0.2 s, roughly half decayed near 1 s, about 80% by 2 s, near 100% at about 4 s. Fig 5.7, unloaded elbow flexion, delay 0.1-0.25 s: close to linear from 0% at 0.1 s to 100% at 0.25 s.
    24	
    25	**Internal conflict, recorded:** the Fig 5.6 caption reads "based on the data of Wilson et al, 1991", but the text gives the 4 s bench-press result to Wilson et al (1990) and the 0.37 s chest/arms result to Wilson et al (1991) (PDF pp. 281-282 / printed pp. 270-271). The curve's near-total decay at about 4 s matches the text's 1990 sentence, not the 0.37 s result. Which year is right is not resolvable from the book.
    26	
    27	The authors' partial resolutions:
    28	- Fibre type (Bosco et al, 1982a): high-FT individuals show the maximum plyometric effect with a short eccentric phase, small range and brief coupling; high-ST individuals jump best with a longer eccentric phase, greater range and longer coupling, "since the actin-myosin cross-bridging attachment time is of greater duration" (PDF p. 282 / printed p. 271).
    29	- Joint-specific maximum delays "probably" exist, but the body has many reflexes acting "at different rates"; tonic (static) and phasic (dynamic) stretch reflexes differ (PDF p. 282 / printed p. 271).
    30	- The weightlifters' "pre-stretch principle" (hold an intense stretch "for a couple of seconds and then thrust") "would seem" to involve the more tonic reflex with longer coupling, and "could certainly not be called plyometric", while phasic reflexes are "more likely" behind classical plyometrics (PDF p. 283 / printed p. 272, verified against the page image).
    31	
    32	**Why it works** — The authors offer fibre type and tonic versus phasic reflexes as explanations, with hedges ("partial solution", "would seem", "more likely"). They do not test either against the conflicting delay data.
    33	
    34	**When to apply** — When someone quotes one fixed "the stretch benefit is gone after X ms" number: the book shows the window depends on the task (unloaded elbow about 0.25 s; loaded bench press up to about 4 s). Inference: for loaded lifts a paused rep still keeps some prestretch benefit for a second or more, per Fig 5.6, while for unloaded fast rebounds the benefit is gone within a few tenths of a second, per Fig 5.7.
    35	
    36	**When NOT to apply** — Do not cite Fig 5.6 under a single Wilson year without noting the caption-text conflict. The figure values are read from small plots and are approximate. Fig 5.7 is Siff's own analysis: the book says it "was derived from some of this work on upper-body non-impact plyometrics", the research "conducted in this field by the author in 1994" (PDF p. 292 / printed p. 281), and gives no subject numbers or publication for it. The fibre-type and reflex explanations are proposals, not demonstrated here.
    37	
    38	**Example** — The authors' own: unloaded explosive elbow flexion loses its prestretch benefit over 0.1-0.25 s (Fig 5.7), while the bench-press benefit decays over about 4 s (Fig 5.6).

plyometrics, because the time taken for the ground reaction force to reach a maximum can be less than 0.15 
second. One also has to take the force-time pattern and the rate of force development (RFD) into account (see Fig 
2.13).
On this scicntific basis, the argument as to whether a given action is classically plyometric or not becomes 
complex and academic, with no real benefit to the prescription of plyometric training. It is better to recognise the 
existence of different types of plyometric training {powermetrics). At the outset, a distinction should be made 
between maximal plyometrics training and sub-maximal plyometric training. In doing so, it is valuable to apply a 
powermetrics intensity scale similar to that used in weightlifting, where exercises arc ranked in terms of 
percentages of one’s 1 RM.
The concept of 1 RMs is meaningless in plyometric training, so one must rely on estimates of muscle tension 
produced by a given drill or on estimates of the impulse (see 5.1) produced during the contact phase of body with 
the ground or projectile. Impulse is equivalent to the change of momentum (m.AV) during the amortisation phase, 
so that its magnitude for a falling body depends on the height from which the body drops. Thus, the momentum 
just before contact (estimated from height of the drop jump or distance fallen by the object) may serve as a 
measure o f intensity. At one end o f the scale lies maximal plyometrics (the equivalent of the emotionally 
demanding competitive maximum, CFmax) and at the other end lies preparatory non-impact plyometrics (see Fig

bounding, shotputting would involve backward rebounds, all forms of jumping would sometimes use one-legged 
hopping forwards, and basketball would involve both short and relatively long amortisation phases in vertical 
rebounds to emulate the different ways of jumping for the basket.
The preparatory or supplementary drills consist of weight training exercises to develop sufficient muscular 
strength (especially eccentric strength) and connective tissue strength and elasticity, as well as varieties of 
######## PDF 285
SUPERTRAINING
Practical application of the plyometric method to different muscle groups is illustrated in the following exercis 
(Fig 5.9). The range of motion should be somewhat greater than the required coordination range of the exercise 
order to enhance shock absorption by the soft tissues and thereby avoid impact injury. With the exampl 
presented as a guideline, an athlete of any specialisation requiring explosive strength can select the necessa 
complex of exercises personally.
The P rescription of P lyom etric E xercise
It is necessary to take into account the following guidelines for using plyometric exercises:
1. The magnitude of the impulsive load is determined by the weight and the height o f its free-fall. The 
optimal combination is determined empirically in each specific case; however, preference should be given 
to a large height over a heavy weight. Since the resulting force is governed by Newton's Second Law (F = 
m.a), a force plate may be used to determine the height of drop to produce the required force.
2. The amortisation phase should be of minimal duration, but sufficient to create impulsive contraction of the 
muscles. Therefore, the initial posture with respect to the joint angles should correspond to the same 
position in which the working movement begins in the sporting exercise.
3. The plyometric training should be preceded by a good warmup of the intensively involved muscles.
4. As an initial guideline, the dosage of plyometric exercises should not exceed 5-8 repetitions in one set. A 
more precise way to determine this is to calculate the force involved (from bodymass and the drop height) 
and the athlete’s level of special speed-strength.
5. One should aim to increase the speed and acceleration of movement before increasing the drop height or 
take-off height.
6. Rest periods are crucial for the effective and safe use of plyometrics. The rest interval between sets of 
maximal plyomctric exercises should be about 10 minutes for power development (strength-speed and 
speed-strength) and much shorter intervals with submaximal plyometrics to develop explosive-strength 
endurance.
In those cases where the plyometric method is used for developing jumping power (i.e. explosive strength and the 
reactive ability of the extensors of the torso and legs), one can work without an additional load and utilise only 
falling bodymass for providing the impulsive stimulation. For example, one may energetically jump upwards, or 
upward and forwards, after a depth-jump from some height (Fig 5.10). The optimal depth o f the jump is 
determined by the athlete's strength fitness, while the athlete should ensure that significant dynamic force is 
developed without slowing down the transition from eccentric to concentric work by the muscles involved.
274

######## PDF 286
The fairly recent adoption of plyometrics by Western coaches as a so-called 'Russian training secret’ has 
created an unwarranted mystique about a method that has been used extensively in Russia since its scientific 
formalisation in the early 1960s as a discrete training system by Verkhoshansky. In recognising that plyometric 
actions are widespread in most sport, Verkhoshansky has always consistently favoured the use of the term 'shock 
method' instead of'plyometrics' to distinguish between naturally occurring plyometric actions in sport and the 
formal discipline he devised as a discrete training system to develop speed-strength in particular. This is why the 
term powermetrics has been suggested elsewhere in this text to refer to plyometric training, as opposed to 
plyometric actions which occur quite naturally in many natural ballistic movements. The earliest published use of 
the word plyometrics seems to have been in a Soviet publication (Zanon, 1966).
Popular adoption of the term 'plyometrics' in the place of'shock method' has produced this confusion, just as 
popular use of the term 'aerobics' has caused widespread confusion between aerobic (cardiovascular) conditioning 
and acrobics as a form of exercise to music. Consequently, it is probably better to refer to plyometric action as 
stretch-shortening action, as has been done in much of the scientific literature, and to redefine 'plyometrics' as a 
specific training system in its own right, or, powermetrics.
Possibly the easiest way of showing that the shock method can indeed be regarded as a separate, goal-directed 
training system is to examine the concept of resistance training. Resistance to movement is encountered in all

{"answer":"GREGORYJ.WILSON

BRUCEC.ELLIOTT

GRAEMEA.WOOD

Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise [23(3):p 364-370, March 1991.](https://www.ovid.com/jnls/acsm-msse/toc/1991/03000)

J., B. C. ELLIOTT, and G. A. WOOD. The effect on performance of imposing a delay during a stretch-shorten cycle movement. Med. Sci. Sports Exerc., Vol. 23, No. 3, pp. 364–370, 1991. Twelve experienced male weight lifters of varying ability completed a series of bench press lifts at 95% of maximum. These lifts included a rebound bench press, which was performed without a delay between the downward and upward components of the lift, a bench press performed without a downward phase, and two bench press movements performed with various pause periods imposed between the downward and upward phases of the lift.
