# The Same Force (F = ma) Produced Different Ways Trains Differently

**What it is** — Newton's second law (F = ma) means the same force can be produced with a
large mass and small acceleration (powerlifting-style, heavy load), a small mass and large
acceleration (many track and field actions), a moderate mass and moderate acceleration
(bodybuilding-style hypertrophy training, roughly 8-12 reps), or near-zero acceleration
under isometric/isokinetic conditions. Despite equal force output, these methods are
argued and shown in practice not to produce the same training effect, because different
neural, muscular, and metabolic processes are engaged in each case. (PDF pp. 32-33,
printed pp. 21-22.)

**Why it works** — The text bases the "do not produce the same results" claim on "practical
experience from three different competitive aspects of strength training" (powerlifting,
weightlifting, bodybuilding; printed 22), not on a stated mechanism. Inference: force alone
does not specify the movement's velocity, duration, muscle action type, or motor unit
recruitment/firing pattern, all of which independently affect the training stimulus; two
efforts that reach the same peak force via different mass-acceleration combinations are

# Before Depth Jumps: Months of Barbell, Jumping, Sprint and Skipping Work, Eccentric and Explosive-Isometric Strength, Static-Start Jumps, Then Low Hops

**What it is** — The authors' preparation rules (pages verified against the page images):
- "Depth-jumps require special preliminary preparation such as a significant volume of barbell exercises and traditional jumping, short sprints and skipping over a period of several months" (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275, item 1). Contra-indications: "Muscle or tendon fatigue, pain or soreness, as well as incompletely healed injuries" (same item).
- "depth-jumping is not a basic type of training to be indulged in lightly by athletes who are relatively unused to explosive or strongly resisted movements. For anyone who is not accustomed to movements such as weightlifting cleans, jerks, squats or hurdling, it is highly advisable that a preparatory programme using submaximal plyometrics, non-impact and non-plyometrics be followed" first (PDF p.
- **Eccentric and explosive-isometric strength first:** "a primary requirement for anyone contemplating the use of classical plyometrics is a high level of eccentric strength and explosive isometric strength. Herein lies the value of small-range squats, power cleans, power snatches, cleans from the hang, snatches from the hang, push presses or jerks, push presses or jerks from racks, and the desce
- **Static start before dynamic start:** "it is initially useful to improve jumping ability from a static start, without exposing oneself to the greater musculotendinous stress of a dynamic start": standing broad and vertical jumps without a dip, then the vertical jump test "progressing from a static flexed knee start to a dynamic dip start with arms flung vigorously upwards" (PDF p. 288 / printed
- **Low hops:** "hopping on the spot at a frequency which feels most comfortable for the athlete, using a few sets of about 25 repetitions", then small forward, backward, sideward, forward-backward and zig-zag hops, then vertical hops "as rapidly as possible, again using a few sets of about 20 repetitions" (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275, item 6). - **Technique and complexity:** learn normal jumping first, with "the correct lumbar-pelvic rhythm, as is also used during clean pulls or power cleans from the ground" (PDF p. 287 / printed p. 276, item 13). "Great caution" with depth jumps involving "one-legged thrusts, changes of direction or complex variations, since the injury risk is significantly higher" (item 14).
- Then integrate: "As eccentric, isometric and concentric strength increases ... the athlete may progress to actions which more rapidly integrate all three aspects of plyometric movement"; the same principles apply to upper-body work (medicine ball catching and throwing, plyometric press-ups and bench presses) (PDF p. 288 / printed p. 277).

- **Basic prescription.** "Repetition work with weights 25-50% of 1RM at a moderate tempo (from 60-120 repetitions/minute) is used for developing strength-endurance. The effectiveness ... will be higher if the work is executed to complete fatigue, although work of shorter duration (60% of the maximal work capacity time) also will yield satisfactory results (Agolinsky, 1953; Korobkov, 1953; Monogarov, 1958; Diachkov, 1961)" (same page).

- **Summary rule.** "multiple repetition exercises with various weights should be considered the fundamental method for developing strength-endurance, with the load being determined by the dynamics of the given exercise. In cases requiring intense effort, an optimally heavy weight should be used together with light weights or with exercises simulating the given sport activity. +# Jumpers Doing 475 Depth Jumps in 12 Weeks Gained More Reactive Ability Than a Group Doing 1472 Barbell Push-Offs and 93 Tons

**What it is** — "The plyometric method of developing explosive strength and reactive ability solves to a significant degree the problem of economising training, since it ensures that a high level of special conditioning is attained in the minimum time. Thus, a comparative experiment revealed that a group of track-and-field jumpers executing primarily depth-jumps (all of them did 475 jumps) over a 12 week period in the preparation phase showed greater improvement in reactive ability than the group which trained with traditional methods and executed 1472 general push-offs (squats, jumping and hopping with a barbell weighing 90-95%, 70-80% and 30-40% of 1RM) and lifted a total volume of 93 tons!" - "*Maximal plyometrics* essentially are low-repetition activities ... Just like maximal strength training with weights, these powerful impulses are not meant to be imposed on the musculature every workout, nor are multiple repetitions even possible or advisable. Moreover, a rest interval of 2-4 minutes is recommended between successive repetitions and as much as 10-12 minutes between sets" (PDF p. 283 / printed p. 272, verified against the page image).

- Prescription item 6: "The rest interval between sets of maximal plyometric exercises should be about 10 minutes for power development (strength-speed and speed-strength) and much shorter intervals with submaximal plyometrics to develop explosive-strength endurance" (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274, verified against the page image).

- "several books advocate sessions with over 100 repetitions of plyometric movements ... This volume of *maximal plyometrics* (unlike sub-maximal plyometrics) is neither productive nor safe for any athlete. Maximal plyometrics, like maximal weight lifting, involves single all-out repetitions separated by a few minutes of rest" (PDF p. 293 / printed p. 282, verified against the page image).
- "classical plyometrics are 1 RM movements which require as much as several minutes of rest before recovery is complete" (PDF p. 294 / printed p. 283, text layer).

- **Impact versus non-impact.** In impact plyometrics "the rebound is stimulated by contact with a surface or object"; in non-impact plyometrics the recoil "is mediated by explosive eccentric action of the muscles that produce a movement not terminated by contact with a surface." Depth jumps are impact; "snap kicks or rapidly-retracted blows in boxing or the martial arts" are non-impact, which "may also be maximal or submaximal."

- **Maximal, submaximal, non-plyometric.** *Maximal plyometrics* are "low-repetition activities where the intensity of the depth jump or rebound exercise is such that maximal or near-maximal rebound tension is produced." *Sub-maximal plyometrics* "do not produce maximal muscular tension, although they are still performed with a minimally long contact phase": "lower box heights are used for depth jumps and the athlete does not strive to reach maximal rebound height"; "rapid double-footed bouncing or low skipping on the spot" are other examples. The three are drawn in one box "as a reminder that there is really a continuum of intensities."

Functional examples: forward bounding for long jump, backward rebounds for shot put, one-legged forward hopping for jumping, and for basketball "both short and relatively long amortisation phases in vertical rebounds." Preparatory or supplementary drills are weight training for muscular strength ("especially eccentric strength") and connective tissue, plus jumping, swinging, throwing and catching drills "with longer duration transition phases"; "Most of the drills described in popular books on plyometrics in the West are actually supplementary exercises."

+# The Lewis Formula P = 21.693 x B x √H Tracks Jump Progress (Inference: It Is Weight Times Mean Free-Fall Speed, Not Take-Off Power)

**What it is** — In the preparatory programme, the authors suggest tracking jump progress this way: "To gain an idea of individual progress, the power developed may be calculated from the Lewis nomogram or from the formula: Power P = (21.693) B√H watts, where B = bodymass in kg and H = height jumped in metres" (PDF p. 288 / printed p. 277, formula read from the page image; the text layer garbles it as "b Vh").

**Why it works** — The book gives no derivation. Inference (physics): 21.693 = 9.8 × √4.9, so the formula is P = B·g·√(g·H/2) with g = 9.8 m/s². A body falling freely from rest through height H reaches √(2gH); its mean speed during the fall is half that, √(gH/2). So the formula is body weight (B·g) times the mean speed of a body falling through H, in watts. It is a fixed function of bodymass and jump height only.

-**When to apply** — As the authors use it: a cheap way to see whether an individual's bodymass-scaled jump is improving over time, when only a jump height and a scale are available. Eric's baseline: jumps are tested on ForceDecks force plates (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 77, the CMJ family protocol). Inference: where force plates are available, measured propulsive power replaces this estimate; the formula is only a fallback.

+**When to apply** — As the authors use it: a cheap way to see whether an individual's bodymass-scaled jump is improving over time, when only a jump height and a scale are available. Eric's baseline: jumps are tested on ForceDecks force plates (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 77, the CMJ family protocol, Inferred (protocol; author uncertain)). Inference: where force plates are available, measured propulsive power replaces this estimate; the formula is only a fallback.

**When NOT to apply** — Inference: because the formula is weight times the mean speed of a free fall through H, it is not the athlete's peak or mean propulsive power during take-off, which depends on how fast force is produced over the push-off distance; two athletes with the same mass and jump height get the same value even if one pushes off much faster. Do not compare its values with force-plate peak power. The book gives no validation data for it.

lines: # Resisted Plyometrics Only Occasionally and Never With Heavy Weights or Stiff Cords in Depth Jumps; Water Plyometrics Are a Safer Submaximal Option
-**What it is** — Under "Resisted and Water Plyometric Training" (PDF pp. 292-293 / printed pp. 281-282; p. 293 verified against the page image, p. 292 from the text layer):
+**What it is** — Under "Resisted and Water Plyometric Training" (PDF pp. 292-293 / printed pp. 281-282; both verified against the page images):

- Resistance can be imposed in the amortisation phase, the concentric rebound or both: light weights, or "elastic cords attached to a harness located near the waist or hips." Both "increase the landing impact and ostensibly increase the strength of reflex muscle contraction", but "also increase the risk of impact and overload injuries and should be applied occasionally with great caution. Even normal running or hurdling with very light weights constitutes a form of loaded plyometric training."

-- Resistance methods "should not use heavy weights or stiff elastic cords during depth jumps, since this increases the coupling time and imposes unnecessarily large loads on the spine and the tendons of the lower extremities, especially during the landing or contact phase."

+- "No resistance methods should not use heavy weights or stiff elastic cords during depth jumps, since this increases the coupling time and imposes unnecessarily large loads on the spine and the tendons of the lower extremities, especially during the landing or contact phase" (sic: the sentence runs across the page break as "No resistance / methods should not use", PDF pp. 292-293 / printed pp. 281-282; the intended sense is clearly "should not").

- Water or "aqua plyometrics" decrease landing force and increase resistance in the recoil. They do "not offer maximal or shock method plyometrics" but serve as preparatory or submaximal plyometrics, "especially for one-legged drills." Water depth sets the resistance: "chest or shoulder high water offering greater resistance during the landing and take-off phases, less intense eccentric muscle activity, smaller impact forces and enhanced safety." Repeated aqua jumps for "rebound explosive muscle endurance" are "considerably safer than their land-based equivalents, though they should not completely replace the latter, since they do not adequately develop the specific neuromuscular patterns or functional needs of explosive sports."

**Why it works** — The authors' reasons are stated: heavy load lengthens the coupling time (taking the drill out of classical plyometrics) and loads spine and tendons; water reduces impact and eccentric intensity.

The authors' partial resolutions:

- Fibre type (Bosco et al, 1982a): high-FT individuals show the maximum plyometric effect with a short eccentric phase, small range and brief coupling; high-ST individuals jump best with a longer eccentric phase, greater range and longer coupling, "since the actin-myosin cross-bridging attachment time is of greater duration" (PDF p. 282 / printed p. 271).

# Fixes applied: Supertraining 5.2.4-5.2.5 (Ch5b), 30 entries

Fixer: Claude Opus. Date: 2026-10-03. Review: `staging/review_supertraining_ch5b_opus.md` (round 1, GO AFTER FIXES: 13 FIX rows, 12 numbered fixes in the verdict list, 5 missing ideas, a Wilson 1990/1991 citation question).
Source checked: `staging/books/supertraining-6th-expanded.pdf`. I extracted the text of PDF idx 233 and 278-299 with PyMuPDF (`staging/_tmp/f5b_text.txt`). I rendered PDF 233, 279, 280, 281, 283, 284, 285, 286, 287, 288, 289, 292, 293, 296, 297 and 299 to `staging/_renders/f5b_p<N>.png`. I opened PDF 233 ("considerably lower"), 281 (margin cut, EM-delay caption), 284 (Fig 5.8, low vs high inertia), 285 (Fig 5.9, prescription list), 287 (Fig 5.11), 292-293 (the "No resistance / methods should not" page break) and 299 (novice experiments). Page key: PDF idx = printed + 11.
Scope: the 30 files in `staging/_scope_supertraining_ch5b.txt`. I edited the 13 flagged entries plus `claim--prestretch-benefit-decay-time-differs-by-task.md` for the Wilson source note. No new entries, so the scope file is unchanged (30 lines). No renames. I did not edit `_book.md`, any 5a or 5c file, or the vault.

| file | what changed |
|---|---|
| claim--high-volume-plyometrics-do-not-build-rebound-fatigue-resistance.md | **Fix 1.** `confidence: contested` is now `supported`. The "Internal conflict, recorded" block is replaced by one sentence: the "futile to rely predominantly" passage is contradicted half a page later, but "that conflict concerns explosive strength, not this entry's Nicol et al (1997) claim, and is recorded in [[heuristic--brief-maximal-tension-vs-plyometrics-by-resistance-size]]". When NOT now says the rating is `supported` because the claim rests on one undescribed citation and nothing in the book contradicts it. The baseline line 122 citation now carries its tag, "Explicit". |
| heuristic--plyometric-surface-footwear-and-simple-apparatus.md | **Fix 2.** `contested` is now `supported`. The "Internal tension" block is replaced with a labelled Inference. It says these are different aims: firm surfaces for maximal rebounds (p. 273), sand for short-term skill gains (p. 278) and soft mats for the no-rebound landing experiment (p. 277). It quotes the text's "as alluded to earlier ..." (PDF 289) to show the sand finding sits beside the soft-surface warning on purpose. It reads "suitably firm shock-absorbing surfaces" (PDF 288) as one instruction. The swing and pogo-stick "no data" flag in When NOT is kept. |
| heuristic--strength-endurance-load-tempo-and-the-75-80-percent-ceiling.md | **Fix 3.** The conflict is now the skater example only (80-85%, Mikhailov & Panov 1975). The rowers' "50-80% of 1RM" is recorded as "at or under the ceiling, so it is not part of the conflict". When NOT now reads "without the 80-85% skater example beside it". The glycolytic inference is rewritten: line 116 (Explicit) "worst case scenario", then "staff do program it in the off-season" (line 117, Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q19). "Inference: to-fatigue strength-endurance sets fit the off-season, not in-season weeks." **Missing idea 2** is added as a **Specificity** bullet quoting PDF 296 / p.285, with a pointer to the Ch3.2.2 taxonomy entry, which already holds the same point from Ch3. |
| heuristic--brief-maximal-tension-vs-plyometrics-by-resistance-size.md | **Fix 4.** (1) The line 76 citation now reads "Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q21)", followed by the baseline's tag verbatim: "[contested; the ratio tracks IMTP strength; one controlled trial (Pleša 2024, basketball, split at 0.90) supported only the strength arm; no football data]". (2) The Example now quotes the p.278 wording, "the resistance is small and the working effect depends upon the reactive ability of the muscles", and adds "The passage names no drill for the second case". "jumping from depth" is removed. (3) When NOT now opens with the novice caveat, scoped to the **within-workout** experiment on PDF 299 ("There was no statistically significant difference ... first two groups"; the depth-jump group gained most). It also notes the separate across-stage experiment on the same page (weights first, then depth jumps, was more effective) and the authors' hedge that "the validity of this hypothesis can be established conclusively only by careful experimentation". Related now links [[case-study--novice-strength-and-speed-strength-sequencing-experiments]]. |
| claim--depth-jump-training-beat-higher-volume-traditional-training-in-jumpers.md | **Fix 5.** The title now says "93 Tons" (the source's word), not "Tonnes". When NOT adds the novice caveat, scoped to the within-workout experiment (PDF 299 / p.288), with the authors' "careful experimentation" hedge. When to apply's sequencing Inference now ends "(for novices, see When NOT to apply)". Related now links the 5c novice entry. |
| heuristic--depth-jump-height-set-by-transition-speed-and-heel-contact.md | **Fix 6.** (1) The baseline sentence now reads: "Eric's baseline: mRSI from daily CMJ testing 'was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker' (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 74, Explicit). Inference: a drop-jump RSI ... at stepped heights would be a separate test of the authors' ... rule; the baseline has no drop-jump test." (2) "considerably lower" is now the full quote "using considerably lower jump heights with anyone who is unused to this type of training" with the locator (Ch4.2.3, PDF p. 233 / printed p. 222, verified against the page image). |
| heuristic--maximal-plyometric-and-depth-jump-volume-and-rest.md | **Fix 7.** (1) Depth-jump item 1 is moved out of Model 2 into its own paragraph, "Depth-jump item 1, kept out of Model 2". It quotes the "complex of vertical jumps (Fig 5.11)" sentence and the Fig 5.11 caption, and says the figure shows ground jumps with no box (verified against the image of PDF 287). It adds "Inference: 'each exercise' most plausibly refers to that complex of ground jumps". "1-15 minutes" is removed from the rest list in The conflict; it stays recorded as printed in the item 1 paragraph and in When NOT. (2) Voices are now labelled per item. Model 1's PDF 283, 293 and 294 statements are "Siff's text" (his term "powermetrics", PDF 279), and item 6 is from the authors' prescription list. In Model 2, item 4 is from the authors' prescription list. Items 2 and 3 are from the "prolific experience" recommendations, whose figures are credited to Verkhoshansky (1977); the list itself carries no citation. (3) Baseline: line 105 now carries its tag, "Inferred (transcript + shared slides)", and the baseline's "Not claimed in the interview". Line 186 is added, "lifting and hard practice end 72 hours before a Saturday game" (Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q15)), with an Inference tying maximal depth-jump sessions to that cut-off. `contested` stays. |
| framework--five-phases-of-a-plyometric-action.md | **Fix 8.** The caption-versus-text paragraph now reads "The caption words the EM delay differently ...", quotes both, and ends "Inference: both describe the electrical-to-mechanical interval." "the book does not reconcile them" is removed. In When NOT, "Do not quote the EM delay definition without noting the caption and text differ" is removed. |
| framework--plyometric-training-classification-impact-intensity-and-function.md | **Fix 9 (classification).** Every "the authors" is now Siff. What it is opens "The text (Siff's classification; it uses his term 'powermetrics', PDF p. 279 / printed p. 268) replaces ...". Why it works, When to apply, When NOT and Example say "Siff's"; the count of "authors" in the file is 0. **Missing idea 1** is added: the full F = ma paragraph from PDF 284 / p.273 (verified against the image), ending "Explosive, low inertia training targets involuntary, neuromuscular and central nervous processes more strongly than high inertia training, which has a greater effect on static strength development and muscle hypertrophy". The entry notes that no study is given and that Ch1's [[principle--equal-force-different-loading-methods]] holds the general equal-force point but not this split. That link is added to Related. |
| heuristic--rate-plyometric-intensity-by-contact-momentum-from-drop-height.md | **Fix 9 (momentum).** "The authors propose" is now "The text (Siff, using his term 'powermetrics', PDF p. 279 / printed p. 268) proposes". "The authors give no numeric scale bands" is now "Siff gives no ...", and "The authors' reasoning" in Why it works is now "Siff's reasoning". 1. **High-volume plyometrics:** applied. Rating changed from contested to supported; the conflict now points to the brief-maximal-tension entry; baseline line 122 tagged Explicit.

4. **Brief maximal tension:** applied, with the novice caveat narrowed.
   - Line 76 now carries its DSI tag verbatim.
   - The Example now quotes the p.278 wording instead of "jumping from depth".
   - The novice caveat names the within-workout experiment on PDF 299 (no significant difference). It also notes the across-stage experiment on the same page, where weights first did work better, and quotes the authors' "careful experimentation" hedge.
   - The 5c novice entry is now linked.
5. **475 jumps:** applied the same way. Title now says "93 Tons"; caveat and link added.
6. **Depth-jump height:** applied. The mRSI sentence is corrected to the readiness marker (line 74); "considerably lower" is now quoted in full with its locator (PDF 233 / printed p.222).
7. **Volume and rest:** applied, with two changes from the review.
   - Item 1 is moved out of Model 2. That it covers only the Fig 5.11 ground jumps is labelled Inference, because "each exercise" can be read either way.
   - Voices are labelled per item, not per model: Siff for the powermetrics passages, "the authors" for the PDF 285 prescription items.
   - Line 105 now shows its Inferred tag, and line 186 is added.
8. **Five phases:** applied. The EM-delay "conflict" is now a wording difference, labelled Inference.
9. **Classification and momentum entries:** applied. The powermetrics passages are now in Siff's voice; prescription items 1 and 4 stay "the authors'".

I also tagged every baseline line cited in the edited files, since the brief requires it.

1. Low vs high inertia went into the classification entry. The Ch1 equal-force entry doesn't hold this split, so I linked it.
2. Strength-endurance specificity went into the ceiling entry, linked to the Ch3.2.2 entry that has the Ch3 version.

The paper is Wilson, Elliott & Wood, *Med Sci Sports Exerc* 1991;23(3):364-370: 12 lifters, bench press at 95%, half-life 0.85 s. It's now a source note in the prestretch entry. The match to Fig 5.6, which suggests the caption's 1991 is right and the text's 1990 wrong, is labelled Inference.
